Senses.Explanation: Literally, a wooden man or wooden figure. The term occurs 940 times in 231 allowlisted texts. Chan verse and teaching-seat speech repeatedly make the inert figure perform human acts: it beckons, speaks, sings, dances, claps a board in the clouds, embroiders a flowered cap at midnight, and converses with the stone woman. One exchange says, 'The wooden man always replies; one with nature cannot speak.' The most stable family pairing is wooden man and stone woman (木人石女), and the pair are made to speak, gesture, sew, sing, or dance. This is where the corpus bends the ordinary object: the impossible acting figure is a stock Chan poetic speaker and actor. The entry records that deployment without assigning a hidden referent to it.
Senses.Note: No passage in the harvested evidence establishes a separate literal puppet or a named person. All examples refer to the same wooden figure under different actions; those actions are not separate senses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat speech pairs the wooden man beckoning with the stone woman nodding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 木人常對語。有性不能言
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An exchange explicitly contrasts the wooden man always replying with one having nature being unable to speak.
A monk frames a question with the wooden man and stone woman together discussing the real.

Occurrences.Kwic: 木人夜半繡花冠，石女天明打破鏡
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A memorial discourse makes the wooden man embroider a flowered cap at midnight and the stone woman break a mirror at dawn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 木人起舞非奇特，石女梳頭越樣新
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse says the wooden man rising to dance is not extraordinary and pairs it with the stone woman combing her hair.
A master answers a question about an auspicious sign with the wooden man clapping a board in the clouds.

Senses.Explanation: Literally a "buddha" (佛) made of "wood" (木): a "wooden buddha," attested 663 times in 181 allowlisted texts. The principal recorded case says Danxia, encountering severe cold at Huilin Temple, took a wooden buddha and burned it. When the superintendent rebuked him, Danxia stirred the ashes and said he was looking for relics. The superintendent replied, "How could a wooden buddha have relics?" Danxia said, "Since it has no relics, bring two more honored ones to burn" (木佛何有舍利，既無舍利，更請兩尊來燒). The phrase also appears in the fixed line "a wooden buddha does not pass through fire" (木佛不度火), alongside a clay buddha not passing through water and a gold buddha not passing through a furnace.
Senses.Note: Later masters repeatedly raise the Danxia case and ask why the superintendent's eyebrows fell out. Recorded answers include "a thief does not raid a poor household" (賊不打貧兒家), "one person transmits a falsehood; ten thousand transmit it as fact" (一人傳虗，萬人傳實), "Zhang drinks the wine and Li gets drunk," and "the cat knows how to climb a tree." The ten occurrences of "What is a wooden buddha?" (如何是木佛) and these later questions retain the literal image as their headword; the texts do not replace it with an abstract category.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃取木佛燒火，向院主呵曰：何得燒我木佛？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Raised Danxia case: he takes a wooden buddha and burns it; the superintendent asks why he burned his wooden buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 院曰：木佛何有舍利？霞曰：既無舍利，更請兩尊來燒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The superintendent says a wooden buddha has no relics; Danxia asks for two more honored ones to burn.
Fixed line in a three-image sequence: a wooden buddha does not pass through fire.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。丹霞燒木佛。院主為甚麼眉鬚墮落。曰。賊不打貧兒家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later question on Danxia burning the wooden buddha receives the answer: a thief does not raid a poor household.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：丹霞燒木佛，院主為甚麼眉鬚墮落？師曰：一人傳虗，萬人傳實。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Another later answer: one person transmits a falsehood; ten thousand transmit it as fact.
